title: Splitwise
scopeHtml: Scope: net balances, split strategies, integer-paise rounding, greedy debt simplification, per-group atomicity and idempotency, undo and audit follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design Splitwise: a group records shared expenses, splits them (equal, exact, percent), tracks who owes whom, and simplifies debts into the fewest payments.

Clarify: split types? Multiple payers per expense? Currency (one)? Rounding rule? Are balances per group or global? Do we need to settle up (record a cash payment)? (Here: one payer per expense, three split types, integer paise, per-group ledger, settle and simplify.)

Worked example. A, B, C. A pays 300.00 for dinner (equal): each owes 100. B pays 150.00 for cab (B and C): each owes 75. C pays 100.00 for tickets (50/30/20 percent). Net: A +150.00, B -55.00, C -95.00 (sums to zero). Simplified: C pays A 95.00, B pays A 55.00. Two payments instead of up to six pairwise debts.

Industry examples. Splitwise's own "simplify debts" feature; Venmo/PhonePe/Google Pay split bills; Tricount, Settle Up. Banks use the same netting idea in clearing houses (many trades net to few transfers).

Everyday analogy. Friends on a trip: instead of everyone repaying everyone, one person collects from those who owe and pays those who are owed.

Common interview traps.

  • Using double for money (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3). Use integer minor units (paise/cents) or BigDecimal.
  • Not saying how leftover paise are handled when 100.00 is split three ways.
  • Storing pairwise debts for every pair (n squared) when a net balance per person is enough.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• SplitStrategy (interface): input total and participants, output a map person to amount owed. Implementations: EqualSplit, ExactSplit, PercentSplit.
  • ExpenseGroup: the ledger. Holds net: Map<user, long> where positive means the group owes the user and negative means the user owes the group.
  • Transfer: from, to, amount; the output of simplify.
  • (Not modelled for brevity: User, Expense history, Group membership; add them as a follow-up for audit and undo.)

Key idea: net balance. Every expense does net[payer] += total and net[participant] -= share. Because the shares sum to the total, the whole ledger always sums to zero (an invariant to assert).

Decision gravity. Keeping only net balances loses "who owes whom for what", so you cannot show per-pair history or per-expense undo. Cheap to keep an append-only expense list alongside (event sourcing style) and derive the net from it. Do that if audit matters; it is reversible if you start with the list.

Everyday analogy. A shared scoreboard where each person has one number: positive means "is owed", negative means "owes".

Common interview traps.

  • Designing the ledger as a graph of edges and then struggling to simplify.
  • Not validating that exact amounts sum to the total and percents sum to 100.

notes.html:

   | SplitStrategy             |
   | split(total, people,      |

     ^          ^           ^

+-------------------------------+      +-------------------+
| ExpenseGroup                  |      | Transfer          |
| net: Map<String,long>         |----->| from, to, amount  |
| lock: ReentrantLock           |      +-------------------+
| addExpense(payer,total,       |

| simplify(): List<Transfer>    |
+-------------------------------+

How to read it. ExpenseGroup never knows how a split is computed; it only applies a Map<user, share>. Adding "split by shares" (2 shares vs 1 share) is one new class.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting split logic in an if/else chain inside addExpense.
  • Forgetting a way to record settlement payments.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy (SplitStrategy): three algorithms behind one signature. Why: split types are the most likely thing to grow (by shares, by itemised bill). Alternative: enum plus switch (fine for 3, painful at 10). Reversible.
  • Greedy algorithm for simplification: repeatedly match the largest creditor with the largest debtor via two priority queues. Each step zeroes at least one person, so at most n - 1 transfers. Note: finding the true minimum number of transfers is NP-hard (it reduces to partitioning into zero-sum subsets); greedy is optimal in practice for interviews and is what people expect. Say that out loud.
  • Invariant checking: sum of net balances is 0; assert it in tests.
  • Rounding rule: EqualSplit gives the first total % n people one extra paisa, so shares sum exactly to the total.

Worked example (rounding). 100.00 over 3 people is 10000 paise: base 3333, remainder 1, so shares are 3334, 3333, 3333. Sum 10000. Splitting as 33.33 x 3 would silently lose a paisa.

Industry examples. Payment ledgers store integer minor units (Stripe amounts are in the smallest currency unit); double-entry accounting is the same "always sums to zero" idea.

Everyday analogy. Settling a tab with the waiter: the person who owes most pays the person who is owed most, then the next pair.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming greedy is provably minimal. It is a good heuristic bounded by n - 1.
  • Percent splits that do not add up after integer division (assign dust to one person).

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (strategies, ledger with simplify, test with a concurrency check):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

/** Money is always long paise/cents. Never double. */
interface SplitStrategy {
    /** Returns who owes how much; the amounts must sum to total. */
    Map<String, Long> split(long total, List<String> participants, List<Long> params);
}

class EqualSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public Map<String, Long> split(long total, List<String> ps, List<Long> params) {
        Map<String, Long> out = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        long base = total / ps.size(), rem = total % ps.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < ps.size(); i++) out.put(ps.get(i), base + (i < rem ? 1 : 0)); // spread leftover paise
        return out;
    }
}

class ExactSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public Map<String, Long> split(long total, List<String> ps, List<Long> amounts) {
        long sum = 0; for (long a : amounts) sum += a;
        if (sum != total) throw new IllegalArgumentException("exact amounts sum " + sum + " != " + total);
        Map<String, Long> out = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < ps.size(); i++) out.put(ps.get(i), amounts.get(i));
        return out;
    }
}

class PercentSplit implements SplitStrategy {
    public Map<String, Long> split(long total, List<String> ps, List<Long> pct) {
        long p = 0; for (long x : pct) p += x;
        if (p != 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("percent must sum to 100");
        Map<String, Long> out = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        long given = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < ps.size(); i++) { long share = total * pct.get(i) / 100; out.put(ps.get(i), share); given += share; }
        String first = ps.get(0);
        out.merge(first, total - given, Long::sum);          // rounding dust goes to the first person
        return out;
    }
}

class Transfer {
    final String from, to; final long amount;
    Transfer(String from, String to, long amount) { this.from = from; this.to = to; this.amount = amount; }
    public String toString() { return from + " pays " + to + " " + amount; }
}

/** One group ledger. net[u] > 0 means the group owes u; net[u] < 0 means u owes the group. */
class ExpenseGroup {
    private final Map<String, Long> net = new HashMap<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    void addExpense(String paidBy, long total, SplitStrategy strategy, List<String> participants, List<Long> params) {
        if (total <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("total must be positive");
        Map<String, Long> shares = strategy.split(total, participants, params);   // validate before touching state
        lock.lock();
        try {
            net.merge(paidBy, total, Long::sum);
            for (Map.Entry<String, Long> e : shares.entrySet()) net.merge(e.getKey(), -e.getValue(), Long::sum);
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    void settle(String from, String to, long amount) {      // 'from' pays cash to 'to'
        lock.lock();
        try { net.merge(from, amount, Long::sum); net.merge(to, -amount, Long::sum); }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    long balanceOf(String u) { lock.lock(); try { return net.getOrDefault(u, 0L); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }

    /** Greedy: biggest debtor pays biggest creditor. At most (people - 1) transfers. */
    List<Transfer> simplify() {
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()));
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> debtors = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()));
        lock.lock();
        try {
            for (Map.Entry<String, Long> e : net.entrySet()) {
                if (e.getValue() > 0) creditors.add(new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(e));
                else if (e.getValue() < 0) debtors.add(new AbstractMap.SimpleEntry<>(e.getKey(), -e.getValue()));
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        List<Transfer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!creditors.isEmpty() && !debtors.isEmpty()) {
            Map.Entry<String, Long> c = creditors.poll(), d = debtors.poll();
            long amt = Math.min(c.getValue(), d.getValue());
            out.add(new Transfer(d.getKey(), c.getKey(), amt));
            if (c.getValue() > amt) { c.setValue(c.getValue() - amt); creditors.add(c); }
            if (d.getValue() > amt) { d.setValue(d.getValue() - amt); debtors.add(d); }
        }
        return out;
    }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExpenseGroup g = new ExpenseGroup();
        List<String> abc = List.of("A", "B", "C");
        g.addExpense("A", 30000, new EqualSplit(), abc, null);          // A paid 300.00, each owes 100
        g.addExpense("B", 15000, new EqualSplit(), List.of("B", "C"), null); // B paid 150, B and C owe 75
        g.addExpense("C", 10000, new PercentSplit(), abc, List.of(50L, 30L, 20L));
        check(g.balanceOf("A") == 30000 - 10000 - 5000, "A net " + g.balanceOf("A"));
        long total = 0; for (String u : abc) total += g.balanceOf(u);
        check(total == 0, "balances must sum to zero");

        List<Transfer> ts = g.simplify();
        ts.forEach(System.out::println);
        check(ts.size() <= 2, "at most n-1 transfers");
        for (Transfer t : ts) g.settle(t.from, t.to, t.amount);
        for (String u : abc) check(g.balanceOf(u) == 0, "all settled " + u);

        // thread-safety: 4 threads add 1000 expenses each, total must stay zero
        ExpenseGroup g2 = new ExpenseGroup();
        Thread[] th = new Thread[4];
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) {
            final String payer = abc.get(t % 3);
            th[t] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) g2.addExpense(payer, 100 + i, new EqualSplit(), abc, null); });
            th[t].start();
        }
        for (Thread t : th) t.join();
        long z = 0; for (String u : abc) z += g2.balanceOf(u);
        check(z == 0, "concurrent total zero");
        System.out.println("P9 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

fun interface SplitStrategy { fun split(total: Long, people: List<String>, params: List<Long>): Map<String, Long> }

val equal = SplitStrategy { total, ps, _ ->
    val base = total / ps.size; val rem = (total % ps.size).toInt()
    ps.withIndex().associate { (i, p) -> p to base + if (i < rem) 1 else 0 }
}

data class Transfer(val from: String, val to: String, val amount: Long)

class ExpenseGroup {
    private val net = HashMap<String, Long>()
    @Synchronized fun addExpense(payer: String, total: Long, s: SplitStrategy,
                                 people: List<String>, params: List<Long> = emptyList()) {
        require(total > 0)
        val shares = s.split(total, people, params)       // validate first
        net.merge(payer, total, Long::plus)
        shares.forEach { (u, amt) -> net.merge(u, -amt, Long::plus) }
    }

    @Synchronized fun simplify(): List<Transfer> {
        val cred = PriorityQueue<Pair<String, Long>>(compareByDescending { it.second })
        val debt = PriorityQueue<Pair<String, Long>>(compareByDescending { it.second })
        net.forEach { (u, v) -> if (v > 0) cred += u to v else if (v < 0) debt += u to -v }
        val out = ArrayList<Transfer>()
        while (cred.isNotEmpty() && debt.isNotEmpty()) {
            val (c, cv) = cred.poll(); val (d, dv) = debt.poll()
            val amt = minOf(cv, dv)
            out += Transfer(d, c, amt)
            if (cv > amt) cred += c to cv - amt
            if (dv > amt) debt += d to dv - amt
        }
        return out
    }
}

Walk-through. Net A +15000, B -5500, C -9500 (paise). Creditors: [A 15000]. Debtors: [C 9500, B 5500]. Step 1: C pays A 9500, A left with 5500. Step 2: B pays A 5500. Done in 2 transfers.

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating the PriorityQueue entry key while it is inside the queue (re-insert after changing, as the code does).
  • Modifying state before the strategy validates, leaving the ledger half-updated on error.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints:
# C pays A 9500
# B pays A 5500
# P9 OK

The test adds three expenses, checks A's balance, asserts all balances sum to zero, runs simplify, applies each transfer through settle and asserts everyone ends at zero. Then 4 threads add 1,000 expenses each and the sum stays zero.

Common interview traps.

  • Only testing happy paths; add exact-split mismatch and percent not equal to 100 (both throw).
  • Test amounts that divide evenly hide rounding bugs; include a 100.00 / 3 case.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Two users add expenses to the same group at the same moment. net.merge on a plain HashMap is not atomic, and a multi-step update (payer plus all shares) must be all-or-nothing, or a concurrent simplify could read a half-applied expense and see balances that do not sum to zero.

  • Chosen: one ReentrantLock per group. Splits are computed outside the lock (pure function), then the ledger update happens in a short critical section. Different groups never contend, since each group has its own lock.
  • Why not ConcurrentHashMap alone? Each merge is atomic, but the set of merges is not; a reader can observe the middle.
  • Alternative: immutable snapshot / copy-on-write. Writers build a new map and swap an AtomicReference; readers never block. Good for read-heavy dashboards.
  • In production the lock is a database transaction: INSERT expense; UPDATE balances in one transaction, with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the group row (or optimistic versioning), so two app servers also serialise. Splitwise-like apps shard by group id, so one group lives on one shard and needs no cross-shard transaction.
  • Idempotency: mobile clients retry. Send an expenseId; a unique constraint rejects the duplicate instead of charging twice.

Incident pattern. Duplicate expenses after a flaky network: user taps "Add" twice. Symptom: double the expected balances and customer complaints. Fix: client-generated idempotency key.

Decision gravity. Shard key = group id is a one-way door (re-sharding is painful) but fits the access pattern: almost every query is within one group.

Everyday analogy. One person holds the group's notebook; only they write in it at a time, so two friends never scribble over the same line.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking a global lock for all groups.
  • Holding the lock while calling the strategy or doing I/O.
  • Updating payer and participants in separate transactions.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Multiple payers per expense: payers become a map of paid amounts; net[p] += paid[p].
  • Itemised bills and tax/tip: split by items, then allocate tax proportionally.
  • Multi-currency: store original currency and a rate at the time; settle in one currency.
  • Undo and edit: keep the expense list; reverse an expense by applying its negation.
  • Global (cross-group) balances between two friends: sum their per-group nets.
  • Recurring expenses (rent): scheduled job adds an expense monthly.
  • Notifications on new expense: reuse the Notification system problem (P8).

Common interview traps.

  • Floating-point percentages like 33.33% that cannot sum to 100.
  • Forgetting that simplifying debts changes "who owes whom" (a user may now pay someone they never met), which some users dislike; offer it as optional.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Store one net balance per person in integer paise; every expense keeps the total at zero.
  • Split types are a Strategy; the leftover paisa goes to the first few people so shares sum exactly.
  • Simplify with two heaps (max creditor vs max debtor): at most n - 1 transfers; true minimum is NP-hard.
  • Make each expense update atomic with a per-group lock (or a DB transaction keyed by group), and use idempotency keys.
  • Keep an append-only expense list if audit, undo or history is required.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the ledger store one net balance per person instead of "who owes whom" for every pair, and what invariant should you assert?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The whole design hinges on this modelling choice; a pairwise graph makes simplification painful.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every expense does net[payer] += total and net[participant] -= share. Shares sum to the total, so the sum of all net balances is always zero: positive means the group owes you, negative means you owe the group. One number per person is enough to settle everything, and it is O(n) memory instead of O(n squared) pairs. The invariant to assert after any operation is that the sum is zero.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A pays 300 (equal, A,B,C): A +200, B -100, C -100       sum 0
B pays 150 (B,C owe 75):   A +200, B -25,  C -175       sum 0

The trade-off is lost detail: net-only cannot show "B owes A 40 for the cab" or undo one expense. Keep an append-only expense list alongside and derive nets from it (event-sourcing style) if audit matters; start with the list and it stays reversible.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Modelling a graph of pair edges, then struggling to simplify.
  • double for money.
  • Not validating that exact amounts sum to the total and percents to 100 before touching state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you record a cash settle-up? -> net[from] += amount, net[to] -= amount; sum still zero.
  2. How do you show per-pair history? -> Derive it from the expense list, not from nets.
  3. Why validate before mutating? -> A failed split must not leave the ledger half-updated.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer builds a debt matrix. The senior reduces it to net balances, asserts the zero-sum invariant, and says what the reduction loses.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Double-entry ledgers in payment systems use the same "always sums to zero" check as a continuous safety net.

questions.promptHtml: How do you simplify a group's debts into as few payments as possible? Is your algorithm optimal?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates a heuristic you can defend from a false claim of optimality.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compute net balances, split into creditors (positive) and debtors (negative), put them in two max-heaps, and repeatedly match the largest creditor with the largest debtor for min(c, d). Each step zeroes at least one person, so there are at most n - 1 transfers. It is not provably minimal: the true minimum is NP-hard (partition into the maximum number of zero-sum subsets). Greedy is what interviews expect and is good in practice.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
net: A +15000, B -5500, C -9500
creditors [A 15000]   debtors [C 9500, B 5500]
C pays A 9500 -> A 5500;  B pays A 5500 -> done in 2 transfers

Why not minimal: if the group splits into two independent zero-sum subsets, n - 2 transfers are possible, which greedy can miss. A person with zero net never takes part. When you mutate an entry while it is inside a PriorityQueue, poll it first, change it, and re-insert.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming greedy is provably minimal.
  • Mutating a key while it is in the heap.
  • Ignoring that simplification may make someone pay a stranger.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Complexity? -> O(n log n).
  2. How would you get the true minimum? -> Subset-sum style DP over zero-sum partitions, exponential in n; acceptable for small groups.
  3. Should simplify change stored data? -> No, it is a read-only suggestion; settlements are recorded separately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "greedy" and stops. The senior bounds it at n - 1, says why optimal is NP-hard, and keeps it a read-only view.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Clearing houses net many trades into few transfers with the same idea.

questions.contextHtml:
A group splits 100.00 three ways and a 100.00 expense by 33.33/33.33/33.34 percent. After both, users see balances like -33.33000000000001 and the ledger sum is 0.01 instead of 0.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
double base = total / ps.size();                    // total is double 100.0
for (String p : ps) out.put(p, round2(base));        // 33.33 each
// percent split
for (int i = 0; i < ps.size(); i++) out.put(ps.get(i), total * pct.get(i) / 100.0);   // pct doubles: 33.33, 33.33, 33.34
val base = total / ps.size                          // total is Double 100.0
ps.forEach { out[it] = round2(base) }               // 33.33 each
ps.indices.forEach { out[ps[it]] = total * pct[it] / 100.0 }
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how should money be represented and split?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use BigDecimal and round half up." Better, but still loses a paisa on three-way splits.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which currency and minor unit? What rounding rule is acceptable (who gets the extra paisa)? Are percentages integers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; repair stored balances by recomputing from the expense list if one exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) binary floating point cannot represent 0.1; (b) 33.33 x 3 = 99.99, one paisa vanishes; (c) fractional percentages that do not sum to 100 exactly.
  4. How I'd verify: Test 100.00 / 3 and assert the shares sum to exactly the total; property test random totals and n.
  5. Root cause: Floating point and no rule for the leftover.
  6. Fix: Store long paise. Equal split: base total / n, remainder total % n, the first rem people get one extra paisa (3334, 3333, 3333). Percent split: integer percent, compute total * pct / 100, and add the rounding dust to one person (the first).

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long base = total / n, rem = total % n;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out.put(ps.get(i), base + (i < rem ? 1 : 0));   // sums exactly to total
val base = total / n; val rem = (total % n).toInt()
ps.withIndex().associate { (i, p) -> p to base + if (i < rem) 1 else 0 }
  1. Prevention: Property test: for any total and any strategy, shares sum to total; lint ban on double in money classes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: BigDecimal is acceptable but needs an explicit scale and rounding mode everywhere; integer minor units are simpler. Do not "fix" by rounding at display time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Who gets the extra paisa fairly? -> Rotate it by expense id or payer-last; the rule only needs to be deterministic.
  • Currencies with 0 or 3 decimals? -> Store minor units per currency (a currency table).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared-expense app drifted by a paisa per split; after six months the group total would not settle to zero until money was moved to integers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps double.
  • Hire: long paise and spreads the remainder.
  • Strong hire: property test, dust rule, percent validation, currency minor units.

questions.contextHtml: Users ask for: (1) an expense paid by two people (A paid 400, B paid 200), (2) an itemised restaurant bill where each item has different participants, with tax and tip split proportionally, and (3) "split by shares" (2 shares for an adult, 1 for a child). Today addExpense(payer, total, strategy, people, params) takes one payer.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, and where do you add each feature without rewriting the ledger?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds three if branches in addExpense and a second payer parameter.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is tax proportional to item subtotals? Rounding rule for proportional allocation? Must the sum of paid amounts equal the total?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; ship shares first, it is a pure new strategy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (designs): (a) multiple payers: change the input to Map<payer, paid>; (b) itemised bills: compute shares per item, then allocate extras proportionally, still output a Map<user, share>; (c) shares: new SplitByShares strategy.
  4. How I'd verify: Property: shares sum to the total, paid sum equals total, ledger sum remains zero; examples with remainders.
  5. Root cause of effort: The ledger only consumes a Map<user, share> and a Map<payer, paid>, so features live in the producers of those maps.
  6. Fix: net[p] += paid[p] for each payer and net[u] -= share[u] for each participant; SplitByShares implements SplitStrategy; itemised bills build a composite strategy. Largest-remainder method to allocate tax and tip so integer amounts sum exactly.
  7. Prevention: Validate sum(paid) == total before applying; golden-file tests for bills.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not extending the enum-and-switch; the strategies stay small and testable. Itemised storage grows the data model, so keep an expense record per bill with its lines.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Taxes rounding makes totals off by a paisa? -> Largest remainder gives the dust to the largest fractional parts.
  • Does the ledger change? -> No; same invariant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A restaurant bill feature was written as a special case inside the ledger and broke simplify; moving it to a share producer fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: branches in addExpense.
  • Hire: new strategy and Map of payers.
  • Strong hire: largest-remainder allocation, validation of paid sum, tests for invariants.

questions.contextHtml:
During a trip, 4 friends add expenses at the same moment. Users occasionally see a dashboard where balances do not sum to zero, and once simplify produced transfers whose total does not match. The ledger is a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> updated with merge for the payer and then for each participant.

t1 addExpense payer=A total=300 -> merge A +300 ... (pause) ... merge B -100 ... merge C -100
t2 simplify() reads net: A=+300, B=0, C=0   (half-applied)
sum(net) = +300  (should be 0)
questions.promptHtml: Why does this happen even though each merge is atomic, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe, so the bug must be elsewhere." Confuses atomic operations with an atomic transaction.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single JVM or many? Are readers allowed to be slightly stale? How hot is one group?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take a consistent snapshot under a lock for simplify and dashboards; recompute from the expense list if there is one.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) multi-step update is not atomic: a reader sees the middle; (b) split validation after partial mutation; (c) read-modify-write on balances across instances. Red herring: hash collisions.
  4. How I'd verify: Stress test: 4 writer threads plus a reader asserting sum == 0 repeatedly; it fails.
  5. Root cause: The invariant spans several keys, but each merge protects only one.
  6. Fix: A ReentrantLock per group around the whole update and around reads (simplify, balanceOf). Compute the split outside the lock (pure), then apply in a short critical section.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Map<String, Long> shares = strategy.split(total, participants, params);   // validate first, no lock
lock.lock();
try {
    net.merge(paidBy, total, Long::sum);
    for (var e : shares.entrySet()) net.merge(e.getKey(), -e.getValue(), Long::sum);
} finally { lock.unlock(); }
val shares = strategy.split(total, people, params)       // validate first, no lock
lock.withLock {
    net.merge(payer, total, Long::plus)
    shares.forEach { (u, amt) -> net.merge(u, -amt, Long::plus) }
}

For read-heavy dashboards: copy-on-write, where writers build a new map and swap an AtomicReference, so readers never block. In production the lock is a DB transaction. 7. Prevention: Invariant assertion in tests with concurrent readers; per-group (not global) locks. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not one global lock (groups never conflict). Not holding the lock while calling the strategy or doing I/O.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two app servers? -> The in-JVM lock does nothing; use a DB transaction with a row lock on the group (or optimistic version), sharded by group id.
  • Deadlock between groups? -> Operations touch one group, so there is no lock ordering problem.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "thread-safe map" ledger showed ghost balances in the UI only during the busiest minute; a snapshot under the group lock fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes ConcurrentHashMap is enough.
  • Hire: lock around the whole multi-key update and around reads.
  • Strong hire: copy-on-write option, DB transaction equivalent, invariant test with a reader.

questions.contextHtml:
Support gets tickets: "Dinner shows up twice, I owe double." Logs for one group (shard g-42), from a mobile client on a flaky train network:

09:12:01.004 POST /groups/g-42/expenses  amount=120000 payer=A   200 OK  (response lost)
09:12:04.900 POST /groups/g-42/expenses  amount=120000 payer=A   200 OK  (client retried)
nets: A=+240000-..., B=-...  (doubled)

About 0.4% of expenses are duplicated on poor networks.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, fix for new data, and clean up existing duplicates safely.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable the retry in the client", which loses expenses when the first request really failed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the client generate an id? Are expenses stored as a list? Is a retry safe to repeat for 24 hours? Do edits exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A "possible duplicate" detector (same group, payer, amount within 10 s) to flag to users, not to auto-delete.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) retry after a lost response created a second row; (b) user double-tapped Add; (c) two devices. Red herring: clock skew.
  4. How I'd verify: Query for expenses in the same group with identical payer/amount/participants within seconds; compare with request ids (none exist today).
  5. Root cause: POST is not idempotent and the client cannot know whether the first request succeeded.
  6. Fix: Client generates expenseId (UUID) per user action and sends it on every retry. The server has a unique constraint (group_id, expense_id); a duplicate returns the stored original result with 200. Inside one transaction: insert the expense, update balances. Cleanup: for flagged pairs, show users a one-tap "delete duplicate" that reverses the expense via its negation, rather than silent deletion.
  7. Prevention: Idempotency keys on every money-moving endpoint; chaos test that drops the response; monitor duplicate-rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not dedupe by content alone (two real 1,200 dinners exist); a key is exact. I would not hard-delete user data without an audit entry.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How long do you keep keys? -> At least the retry window (for example 24 h to 7 days); the unique constraint on expense id lives forever since it is the row id.
  • Same key, different body? -> Reject with 409; it is a client bug.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments-like feature doubled thousands of entries during a holiday weekend; adding a client-generated id and a unique constraint made retries harmless.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: remove retries or dedupe by amount.
  • Hire: idempotency key with unique constraint and one transaction.
  • Strong hire: safe cleanup through reversal, 409 on mismatched body, monitoring and chaos test.

questions.contextHtml: Today each group stores only net balances (one table, 8M groups, 600 writes/s). Product wants undo and edit of expenses plus an audit trail. Expense history exists nowhere. You must migrate without downtime, and some groups are written by two app versions during a rolling deploy.
questions.promptHtml: How do you get to an append-only expense log, and how do you roll it out and verify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an expenses table and backfill it overnight", ignoring writes during the migration and the old nets that have no source.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we have old requests logged anywhere? Can we accept that pre-migration history is lost (opening balance)? What read paths use nets? Can writes pause per group?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is planned. I would snapshot the nets first for rollback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (strategies): (a) opening-balance entries: one synthetic "opening balance" expense per user from today's nets, then log everything after; (b) dual-write nets and log, compare; (c) cut over reads to derive nets from the log.
  4. How I'd verify: For each group, sum(log deltas) + opening == stored net as a continuous check (shadow comparison); a mismatch rate dashboard; per-group zero-sum assertion.
  5. Root cause of risk: Changing the source of truth while writers run.
  6. Fix (phases): (1) create log table with a unique expense_id; write opening balances; (2) deploy dual-write: in one transaction insert the log row and update net; (3) compare in shadow for a week; (4) switch reads that need history to the log; (5) make the log the source of truth and nets a cached projection; (6) enable undo (reversal entries, never deletes). Roll out by group shard; feature flag per group.
  7. Prevention: Idempotent migration steps, backfill batches with rate limits, rollback plan: nets are still correct until phase 5.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The "opening balance" loses history for old expenses; tell users. I would not rewrite nets from a backfill that could miss in-flight writes. One-way door: once the log is the truth, reverting needs a rebuild, so go slowly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two app versions during deploy? -> Version-compatible writes: old version updates nets only; reconciliation job fills missing log entries as "unknown" until old code is gone.
  • Storage growth? -> 600 writes/s is about 52M rows/day; partition by group or time and archive old partitions (verify sizing).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team switched the source of truth in one release and found 0.1% of groups out of balance; the shadow comparison phase would have caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: overnight backfill.
  • Hire: dual-write, shadow comparison, opening balance.
  • Strong hire: phases with rollback, mixed-version deploy handling, reversal-based undo, sizing.

questions.contextHtml: PM: "Make debts simpler across all my friends, not just per group." Users also complained: "After Simplify, the app says I should pay Dev, someone I have never met." A group of 12 has nets: A +900, B +300, C -200, D -250, E -400, F -350, and the rest 0. The PM wants one screen with "who do I pay".
questions.promptHtml: Ask your clarifying questions, then propose behaviour, algorithm and the data you would store.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Runs the greedy across everything globally and ignores trust, currency, and partial netting rules.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should simplify cross group boundaries or only within a group? Is paying a stranger acceptable (opt-in)? Do different groups have different currencies? Is the goal fewer payments or lower friction? Do settled payments need confirmation from the receiver?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make simplification optional per group, defaulting to "off", and show the original pairwise "who owes whom" next to it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): (a) simplify within a group only (safe); (b) global per-pair netting: for two friends, sum their per-group nets (they already know each other); (c) global greedy across all friends (fewest payments, but strangers pay each other); (d) friend-graph constrained simplification.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare options on real data: number of transfers saved vs fraction of transfers between non-friends.
  5. Root cause of the conflict: Fewest transfers and "pay people I know" are different objectives; the minimum is NP-hard anyway, so heuristics are a product choice.
  6. Fix: Default: per-group greedy simplification (at most n - 1 transfers). For the global screen: compute per-pair net across groups (sum of per-group pairwise debts derived from the expense log), then offer an optional, opt-in simplified view restricted to existing friend edges. Worked example: nets A +900, B +300, C -200, D -250, E -400, F -350 give at most 5 transfers: E->A 400, F->A 350, D->A 150, D->B 100, C->B 200.
  7. Prevention: Settlement confirmation flow; show the reason ("this saves 4 payments"); tests asserting totals and that nets reach zero.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not claim the global result is minimal. Multi-currency netting across groups needs a rate at the time of expense; keep currencies separate unless users convert.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Receiver disagrees about a payment? -> Settlement is a two-party event; the payer proposes, the receiver confirms.
  • Does simplify alter stored debts? -> No: it is a view; only recorded settlements change nets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "simplify everything" release produced the most complaints of the year; making it opt-in per group and friend-restricted reduced them to almost none.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: global greedy, no questions.
  • Hire: clarifies, offers per-group default and optional global view.
  • Strong hire: separates objectives, per-pair cross-group netting from the log, settlement confirmation, works the numbers.
